The equation of the line $l_{1}$ is $y = 3x + 2$ and $l_{2}$ is perpendicular to $l_{1}$. What is the equation of $l_{2}$?

$y =$
{{field-1}}
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, the slope of ${l}_{2}$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of ${l}_{1}.$ Since ${l}_{1}$ has a slope of $3,$ the line ${l}_{2}$ must have a slope of $-\frac{1}{3}.$

Our perpendicular line must have the slope $m=-\frac{1}{3}$ and a $y$-intercept of $2.$ Therefore, it can be written in slope-intercept form as

$$
y=-\frac{1}{3}x+2.
$$

question.:question/problem: The lines $y=\frac{1}{2}x-3$ and $y=mx+b$ are perpendicular. Given that the line $y=mx+b$ passes through the point $(-1,5),$ what is the value of $b?$
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let ${l}_{1}$ denote the line $y=\frac{1}{2}x-3,$ and let ${l}_{2}$ denote the line we want to find.

Since perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, the slope of ${l}_{2}$ is the negative reciprocal of the slope of ${l}_{1}.$ Since ${l}_{1}$ has a slope of $\frac{1}{2},$ the line ${l}_{2}$ must have a slope of $-2.$

Our perpendicular line must have the slope $m=-2$ and pass through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(-1,5).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-5 & =-2(x-(-1)) \\ y-5 & =-2(x+1) \\ y-5 & =-2x-2 \\ y & =-2x+3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $b=3.$

Our perpendicular line must have the slope $m=-\frac{5}{2}$ and pass through the point $({x}_{1},{y}_{1})=(4,-4).$ Using point-slope form and simplifying, we obtain the equation of the line in slope-intercept form:

$$
\begin{aligned}y-{y}_{1} & =m(x-{x}_{1}) \\ y-(-4) & =-\frac{5}{2}(x-4) \\ y+4 & =-\frac{5}{2}x+10 \\ y & =-\frac{5}{2}x+6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $b=6.$
